title: CNS and PNS: the two halves
objective: Separate the central and peripheral nervous systems and place the DRG correctly.

steps.title: Two compartments
steps.body:
The nervous system splits into two:

- **[[CNS]]** — the brain and spinal cord, where signals are integrated.
- **[[PNS]]** — the nerves and [[ganglion|ganglia]] outside them that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.

The divide isn't just location; it changes the cell neighborhoods, the support cells, and the rules for regeneration.

steps.title: Where the DRG sits
steps.body: The [[DRG]] is a **PNS** structure: a cluster of sensory cell bodies just outside the spinal cord. Its neurons straddle the border — one axon branch reaches far into the body (skin, gut, pancreas), the other enters the CNS at the spinal cord. That border-straddling is why the DRG is such a useful access point.

steps.prompt: Which structure is part of the CNS?
steps.explanation: The spinal cord (with the brain) is the CNS. Ganglia and named nerves — including the DRG, sciatic, and vagus — are PNS.

steps.prompt: Why does the CNS/PNS distinction matter for your work?
options: PNS neurons like DRG cells are accessible from the body (organ injections, nerve recordings) in ways CNS neurons aren't
The PNS can't be studied in mice
steps.explanation: Because DRG afferents are peripheral, you can reach them from the organ they innervate — the basis for retrograde labeling and the pancreas injections in your project.

reviewNotes: Orients the whole D track; places the DRG for later lessons.
